claim: Phenazines are natural bacterial antibiotics that can protect crops from disease.
source: Phenazines are natural bacterial antibiotics that can protect crops from disease.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general property of phenazines, supported by established scientific knowledge about these compounds.

claim: All known phenazine producers contain the core phenazine biosynthesis genes phzA/BCDEFG, almost always in single-copy.
source: Because all known phenazine producers contain the core phenazine biosynthesis genes, phzA/BCDEFG, almost always in single-copy, we reasoned that given a sufficiently broad database of these proteins, we could accurately identify and enumerate the levels of phz+ bacteria via shotgun-metagenomics (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge in the field and is the basis for the methodological approach used in the study.

claim: A comprehensive phenazine biosynthesis reference database was constructed containing 181 phenazine producer genomes.
source: In total, we assembled a list of 181 phenazine producer genomes (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the data generated in this study.

claim: The final reference set contained 100 proteobacterial and 81 actinobacterial genomes representing a total of 15 phylogenetic Orders.
source: The final reference set contained 100 proteobacterial and 81 actinobacterial genomes representing a total of 15 phylogenetic Orders, exemplifying the diversity of phenazine producers (Figure 1C; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data generated in the study and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Species organization in the phenazine biosynthesis phylogenetic tree substantially differs from the known phylogenetic relationship of phz+ bacteria.
source: Notably, species organization in this tree substantially differ from the known phylogenetic relationship of phz+ bacteria in our database.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the phylogenetic analysis presented in the study.

claim: Multiple horizontal gene transfer (HGT) events have likely shaped the evolution of phenazine biosynthesis.
source: These results support and expand on previous smaller scale analyses made with the phzF gene (Mavrodi et al., 2010), and suggest that multiple horizontal gene transfer (HGT) events have likely shaped the evolution of phenazine biosynthesis.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the phylogenetic patterns observed and supported by previous literature.

claim: The computational approach accurately captures the total phz+ bacteria level even in communities that contain more than one producer.
source: Importantly, our simulations capture the total phz+ bacteria level even in communities that contain more than one producer (Figure 2B) and the relative proportions of these different phz+ bacteria are measured with low error (Figure 2C–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the simulation data presented in Figure 2B-D.

claim: The approach could identify as little as 0.1% phz+ bacteria, even in relatively low coverage metagenomic samples (5–10M reads).
source: In addition, our approach could identify as little as 0.1% phz+ bacteria, even in relatively low coverage metagenomic samples (5–10M reads) and detected no producers in any of the negative controls (Figure 2B; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the simulation validation data shown in the figures.

claim: The number of phz+ pseudomonads in wheat rhizosphere was estimated at 6.5 × 10^6 cfu/g roots and at 1.6 × 10^3 cfu/g in bulk soil.
source: The number of phz+ pseudomonads was determined using a culturing-based approach and was estimated at 6.5 × 106 cfu/g roots in the wheat rhizosphere and at 1.6 × 103 cfu/g in bulk soil, in agreement with previous reports (Mavrodi et al., 2018).
evidence: This is experimental data from culturing experiments conducted in this study.

claim: Metagenomic analysis found an average relative abundance of 1.1% (± 0.4%) phz+ bacteria in wheat seedling rhizosphere and 0.32% (± 0.14%) in bulk field soil.
source: In agreement with the culturing results, we find clear signal representing phz+ bacteria in these samples, with an average relative abundance of 1.1% (+ / - 0.4%) in the wheat seedling rhizosphere and 0.32% (+ / - 0.14%) of the bulk field soil microbiome (Figure 3A; Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is metagenomic data from the field validation study.

claim: Two different bacterial clades occur at roughly the same abundance in wheat rhizosphere: fluorescent pseudomonads and Streptomyces spp.
source: Surprisingly, a closer examination of the phz+ bacteria in our rhizosphere metagenomes showed that two different bacterial clades occur at roughly the same abundance in this niche: the expected, culture-validated fluorescent pseudomonads, and Streptomyces spp., which were not previously known to occur in meaningful levels in this environment (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a novel finding from the metagenomic analysis presented in the study.

claim: Combining the average phz+ pseudomonad cfu/g with their average estimated percent out of all bacteria suggests a wheat seedling rhizosphere bacterial load of ~10^9 bacteria per gram roots.
source: Indeed, combining the average phz+ pseudomonad cfu/g with their average estimated percent out of all bacteria suggests a wheat seedling rhizosphere bacterial load of ~109 bacteria per gram roots, in agreement with other rhizosphere load estimates (Bakker et al., 2013; Mavrodi et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an inference based on combining culturing and metagenomic data, validated by comparison to literature.

claim: More than 28% (229/807) of all samples analyzed contained at least 0.25% phz+ bacteria in their microbiome.
source: Estimated phz+ levels range from 0% to 2.7% of total environmental bacteria, with >28% (229/807) of all samples containing at least 0.25% phz+ bacteria in their microbiome (Figure 4A; Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is a summary statistic from the global metagenomic analysis.

claim: There is a 1.9-fold higher average phz+ level in rhizospheres compared to bulk soils.
source: Notably, we find a 1.9-fold higher average phz+ level in rhizospheres compared to bulk soils (Figure 4A; p=4.2×10−17; Wilcoxon).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the global metagenomic analysis with a p-value indicating significance.

claim: Samples with high total producer levels (at least 0.5% phz+) are 8.9-fold enriched in samples annotated as rhizosphere compared to bulk soil.
source: Furthermore, samples with high total producer levels (at least 0.5% phz+) are 8.9-fold enriched in samples annotated as rhizosphere compared to bulk soil.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the global metagenomic analysis.

claim: Higher phz+ levels are particularly common in crops such as sugarcane, wheat, barley, maize, and citrus, as well as the model plant Arabidopsis thaliana.
source: Higher phz+ levels are particularly common in crops such as sugarcane, wheat, barley, maize, and citrus, as well as the model plant Arabidopsis thaliana (Figure 4A; Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is a finding from the global metagenomic analysis showing crop-specific patterns.

claim: phz+ Streptomyces represent a major portion of phz+ bacteria in most habitats.
source: Strikingly, we find that phz+ Streptomyces represent a major portion of phz+ bacteria in most habitats (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a finding from the taxonomic analysis of the metagenomic data.

claim: phz+ Streptomyces are detected in substantial levels in over 67% (154/229) of phz+ rich samples (containing at least 0.25% phz+ bacteria).
source: Furthermore, phz+ Streptomyces are detected in substantial levels in over 67% (154/229) of phz+ rich samples (containing at least 0.25% phz+ bacteria), both soil and rhizosphere derived (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the taxonomic analysis.

claim: Xanthomonadales phz+ bacteria were detected in 22% (50/229) of phz+ rich samples.
source: Surprisingly, we detected Xanthomonadales phz+ bacteria in 22% (50/229) of our phz+ rich samples (Figure 4—figure supplement 2; Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a finding from the taxonomic analysis of the metagenomic data.

claim: High levels of Xanthomonadales phz+ bacteria occur exclusively in plant rhizosphere microbiomes, preferentially colonizing maize, citrus, sugarcane, and A. thaliana.
source: High levels of these phz+ bacteria occur exclusively in plant rhizosphere microbiomes, preferentially colonizing maize, citrus, sugarcane, and A. thaliana (Figure 4B; Figure S5).
evidence: This is a finding from the taxonomic and habitat analysis of the metagenomic data.

claim: Xanthomonadales bacteria represent the most abundant species in the data, reaching up to 2.7% of all bacteria in the maize rhizosphere.
source: In addition to their notable distribution, Xanthomonadales bacteria represent the most abundant species in our data, reaching up to 2.7% of all bacteria in the maize rhizosphere (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is a finding from the metagenomic analysis showing the maximum abundance observed.

claim: 21 samples contain substantial levels of phdA+ bacteria (at least 0.25%).
source: While we find scarce evidence for the podA pyocyanin oxidative demethylation gene (Costa et al., 2017) in these soil and plant environments, 21 samples contain substantial levels of phdA+ bacteria (at least 0.25%; Supplementary file 4), whose gene product begins the degradation of PCA (Costa et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a finding from the phenazine degradation gene analysis.

claim: 71% (15/23) of samples with phdA+ bacteria were annotated as switchgrass rhizospheres.
source: Notably, 71% (15/23) of these samples were annotated as switchgrass rhizospheres, with six samples also containing similar or higher phz+ bacterial levels composed of mostly Streptomyces (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the phenazine degradation gene analysis showing habitat specificity.

claim: Metagenomic sequencing data almost exclusively maps to Dyella rather than Lysobacter among Xanthomonadales.
source: Strikingly, we find that our metagenomic sequencing data almost exclusively maps to Dyella rather than Lysobacter (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a finding from the taxonomic analysis of Xanthomonadales.

claim: D. japonica is likely to produce phenazines that are similar or identical to those previously detected in L. antibioticus.
source: Thus, D. japonica is likely to produce phenazines that are similar or identical to those previously detected in L. antibioticus (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is an inference based on genomic comparison between D. japonica and L. antibioticus.

claim: WT D. japonica produces a bright orange pigment when grown in minimal medium for 48 hr, while both mutant cultures (ΔphzA and ΔphzT) remain completely colorless.
source: Indeed, while WT D. japonica produce a bright orange pigment when grown in minimal medium for 48 hr, both mutant cultures remain completely colorless, indicating that they are phenazine deficient (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is experimental data from the phenazine production assay.

claim: D. japonica produces the precursor PDC, and the potent antimicrobials myxin and a reduced myxin derivative (1-Hydroxy-6-methoxyphenazine-N10-oxide).
source: These included the precursor PDC, and the potent antimicrobials myxin and a reduced myxin derivative (1-Hydroxy-6-methoxyphenazine-N10-oxide) (Chowdhury et al., 2012; Weigele et al., 1970; Figure 5D; Figure 5—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is experimental data from LC-MS analysis identifying specific phenazines.

claim: The conserved transcription factor deleted in the analysis (phzT) is an essential regulator of phenazine biosynthesis in D. japonica.
source: These results suggest that the conserved transcription factor deleted in our analysis is an essential regulator of phenazine biosynthesis in this organism.
evidence: This is an inference based on the phenotype of the ΔphzT mutant.

claim: D. japonica upregulates phenazine biosynthesis during phosphate limitation.
source: Perhaps not surprisingly, therefore, we find similar induction of phenazine biosynthesis in phosphate limited D. japonica cultures, even after only 24 hr (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is experimental data from the phosphate limitation experiment.

claim: D. japonica accumulates to high levels in the maize mono-colonization model, reaching an average of 1.5 × 10^6 cfu/mg root-base.
source: We find that D. japonica accumulates to high levels in this mono-colonization model, reaching an average of 1.5 × 106 cfu/mg root-base (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is experimental data from the gnotobiotic maize colonization assay.

claim: Phenazine-deficient mutants accumulate to a slightly higher level (1.5-fold; p=0.013) than wild-type D. japonica in the maize colonization model.
source: We note that phenazine-deficient mutants accumulate to a slightly higher level (1.5-fold; p=0.013; t-test) (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is experimental data from the gnotobiotic maize colonization assay with statistical significance.

claim: D. japonica colonizes the root interior and root hair tips of maize seedlings.
source: Bacterial HCR signal indicative of microaggregate formation was readily visible within the root inner compartment is readily detected (Figure 6D). In addition, root hair tips appeared to be preferentially colonized by D. japonica (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is experimental data from the in situ imaging of bacterial colonization.

claim: Phenazine biosynthesis is a highly prevalent trait that is enriched in plant microbiomes relative to bulk soils.
source: We developed and field-validated a computational method to analyze >800 metagenomes from across the world and show that phenazine biosynthesis is a highly prevalent trait that is enriched in plant microbiomes relative to bulk soils.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the global metagenomic analysis.

claim: Known phenazine biodegradation genes are rarely detected in soil and plant-associated environments.
source: In contrast, known phenazine biodegradation genes are rarely detected in these environments.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the global metagenomic analysis of degradation genes.

claim: Phenazines are heterotricyclic N-containing metabolites mainly produced by bacteria in soil and plant-root microbiomes.
source: Phenazines are heterotricyclic N-containing metabolites mainly produced by bacteria in soil and plant-root microbiomes (Biessy and Filion, 2018; Mavrodi et al., 2010), though some are also important in chronic human infections (Sismaet et al., 2016; Wilson et al., 1988).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Phenazines act as broad-spectrum antibiotics by generating toxic reactive oxygen species (ROS) as well as interfering with cellular respiration chains.
source: Members of this diverse family of redox-active metabolites act as broad-spectrum antibiotics by generating toxic reactive oxygen species (ROS) as well as interfering with cellular respiration chains (Baron et al., 1989; Perry and Newman, 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge about phenazine mechanisms supported by citations.

claim: Phenazines can promote survival under anoxic conditions.
source: In addition to their activity as antibiotics, phenazines can benefit their producers in other ways: promoting survival under anoxic conditions (Glasser et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2010), facilitating biofilm development (Dietrich et al., 2013) and iron acquisition (Wang et al., 2011), and increasing the fitness of phenazine-producing (phz+) fluorescent pseudomonads in the plant rhizosphere (LeTourneau et al., 2018; Mazzola et al., 1992).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Phenazines can facilitate biofilm development.
source: In addition to their activity as antibiotics, phenazines can benefit their producers in other ways: promoting survival under anoxic conditions (Glasser et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2010), facilitating biofilm development (Dietrich et al., 2013) and iron acquisition (Wang et al., 2011), and increasing the fitness of phenazine-producing (phz+) fluorescent pseudomonads in the plant rhizosphere (LeTourneau et al., 2018; Mazzola et al., 1992).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Phenazines can facilitate iron acquisition.
source: In addition to their activity as antibiotics, phenazines can benefit their producers in other ways: promoting survival under anoxic conditions (Glasser et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2010), facilitating biofilm development (Dietrich et al., 2013) and iron acquisition (Wang et al., 2011), and increasing the fitness of phenazine-producing (phz+) fluorescent pseudomonads in the plant rhizosphere (LeTourneau et al., 2018; Mazzola et al., 1992).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Phenazines can increase the fitness of phenazine-producing (phz+) fluorescent pseudomonads in the plant rhizosphere.
source: In addition to their activity as antibiotics, phenazines can benefit their producers in other ways: promoting survival under anoxic conditions (Glasser et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2010), facilitating biofilm development (Dietrich et al., 2013) and iron acquisition (Wang et al., 2011), and increasing the fitness of phenazine-producing (phz+) fluorescent pseudomonads in the plant rhizosphere (LeTourneau et al., 2018; Mazzola et al., 1992).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Phenazines produced by fluorescent pseudomonads have been shown to protect major crops such as wheat and tomato from disease-causing fungi and water molds.
source: In the context of the plant microbiome, phenazines produced by fluorescent pseudomonads have been shown to protect major crops such as wheat (Chen et al., 2018; Thomashow et al., 1990) and tomato (Chin-A-Woeng et al., 1998) from disease-causing fungi and water molds.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Naturally produced phenazine 1-carboxylic acid (PCA) measured in commercial wheat rhizospheres reached levels as high as 1 µg PCA per gram fresh roots.
source: Moreover, naturally produced phenazine 1-carboxylic acid (PCA) measured in commercial wheat rhizospheres reached levels as high as 1 µg PCA per gram fresh roots, and strongly correlated with the number of cultured phz+ pseudomonads (Mavrodi et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies supported by citation.

claim: The pathogenic fungus, Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. radicis-lycopersici, was previously shown to colonize similar tomato root zones as plant-growth promoting phz+ pseudomonads.
source: Interestingly, the pathogenic fungus, Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. radicis-lycopersici, was previously shown to colonize similar tomato root zones as plant-growth promoting phz+ pseudomonads, where they likely compete for plant-root exudates (Bolwerk et al., 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies supported by citation.

claim: Phenazine-producing bacteria are positively correlated with warmer and more arid soils and lower species diversity.
source: Phenazine-producing bacteria are positively correlated with warmer and more arid soils and lower species diversity (Maestre et al., 2015; Mavrodi et al., 2012), suggesting that in a warming climate, phenazine production may impact the composition of the microbial communities associated with certain crops.
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies supported by citations.

claim: Phenazines can be degraded and consumed by other soil bacteria.
source: However, phenazines can also be degraded and consumed by other soil bacteria (Costa et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: All producer genomes contain a conserved set of core biosynthesis genes phzA/BCDEFG.
source: Despite this diversity, all producer genomes contain a conserved set of core biosynthesis genes phzA/BCDEFG (Biessy and Filion, 2018; Mavrodi et al., 2010; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The core biosynthesis proteins synthesize one of two main phenazines that act as precursors for all other derivatives: PCA in pseudomonads and phenazine-1,6-dicarboxylic acid (PDC) in most other species.
source: Together, these proteins synthesize one of two main phenazines that act as precursors for all other derivatives: PCA in pseudomonads and phenazine-1,6-dicarboxylic acid (PDC) in most other species (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is established knowledge shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Phenazine chemical diversity is determined by specific auxiliary genes, which modify and decorate the core phenazine structure.
source: Phenazine chemical diversity is determined by specific auxiliary genes, which modify and decorate the core phenazine structure.
evidence: This is established knowledge about phenazine biosynthesis.

claim: Phenazine modifications can strongly affect the toxicity spectrum and function of different phenazine species.
source: These modifications can strongly affect the toxicity spectrum and function of different phenazine species (Laursen and Nielsen, 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Highly similar copies of the phzC gene were common in non-producer genomes.
source: During this analysis, we noticed that highly similar copies of the phzC gene were common in non-producer genomes and therefore removed this gene from our analysis.
evidence: This is an observation made during the database construction process.

claim: Pseudomonas species are highly clustered in the phenazine biosynthesis phylogenetic tree.
source: While Pseudomonas species are highly clustered, other clades form surprising groupings.
evidence: This is an observation from the phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Phenazine-biosynthesis actinobacterial sequences of the Micrococcales order are more similar to those from proteobacteria of the Enterobacterales, Myxococcales and Vibrionales orders.
source: For example, phenazine-biosynthesis actinobacterial sequences of the Micrococcales order (e.g., Brevibacterium linens) are more similar to those from proteobacteria of the Enterobacterales, Myxococcales and Vibrionales orders (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is an observation from the phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Burkholderiales and Xanthomonadales are both embedded deep within the actinobacterial part of the phenazine biosynthesis tree rather than near other proteobacteria.
source: In addition, Burkholderiales and Xanthomonadales are both embedded deep within the actinobacterial part of the tree rather than near other proteobacteria (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is an observation from the phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The approach accurately captures the levels of phz+ and phenazine-degrading bacteria in simulated communities across a wide range of abundances and library coverages.
source: We find that this approach accurately captures the levels of phz+ and phenazine-degrading bacteria (Mycobacterium fortuitum CT6) in the same simulated communities and across a wide range of phdA+/podA+ bacterial abundances, and library coverages (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a validation result from the simulation analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Three species in the reference set comprise >87% of the phz+ Pseudomonas rhizosphere sequencing reads.
source: Notably, three species in our reference set comprise >87% of the phz+ Pseudomonas rhizosphere sequencing reads (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a finding from the taxonomic analysis of the wheat rhizosphere samples.

claim: Pseudomonas chlororaphis aureofaciens 30-84 contains an adjacent phzO modification gene, suggesting that pseudomonads in this environment produce PCA and 2-hydroxyphenazine-1-carboxylic acid (2-OH-PCA).
source: Whereas these P. fluorescens and P. orientalis genomes contain a solo phzA/BCDEFG operon, Pseudomonas chlororaphis aureofaciens 30-84 also contains an adjacent phzO modification gene, suggesting that pseudomonads in this environment produce PCA and 2-hydroxyphenazine-1-carboxylic acid (2-OH-PCA) (Delaney et al., 2001).
evidence: This is an inference based on genomic analysis and supported by citation.

claim: The Streptomyces mapped reads mapped to many species rather than just a few genomes, as seen for Pseudomonas.
source: The Streptomyces mapped reads in our data mapped to many species rather than just a few genomes, as seen for Pseudomonas (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a finding from the taxonomic analysis of the wheat rhizosphere samples.

claim: Three main Streptomyces groups occupy the wheat rhizosphere.
source: Nevertheless, binning these Streptomyces genomes according to similarity in their phenazine genomic regions revealed that three main groups occupy the wheat rhizosphere (Figure 3D–E).
evidence: This is a finding from the taxonomic and genomic analysis of the wheat rhizosphere samples.

claim: The phz+ Streptomyces community is likely to produce multiple chemically diverse phenazines in the wheat rhizosphere environment.
source: These data imply that in contrast to pseudomonads, the phz+ Streptomyces community is likely to produce multiple chemically diverse phenazines in this environment, some of which await description.
evidence: This is an inference based on the genomic analysis of Streptomyces phenazine biosynthesis genes.

claim: The metagenomic-based approach was applied to 799 publicly available shotgun-metagenomes.
source: To acquire a more complete picture of phenazine biosynthetic and catabolic potentials in soils and crop rhizospheres, we applied our approach to an additional 799 publicly available shotgun-metagenomes (Supplementary file 4; Methods).
evidence: This is a description of the data analyzed in the study.

claim: The samples were broadly classified as either soil (58.7%; 474/807) or rhizosphere (41.3%; 333/807).
source: These new samples were combined with the eight wheat and field soil samples described above and were broadly classified as either soil (58.7%; 474/807) or rhizosphere (41.3%; 333/807).
evidence: This is a description of the sample classification in the study.

claim: In almost all cases, phz+ Streptomyces can be found along with other producers from different clades, including various actinobacteria and proteobacteria.
source: In almost all cases, phz+ Streptomyces can be found along with other producers from different clades, including various actinobacteria and proteobacteria (Figure 4—figure supplement 2; Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is a finding from the taxonomic analysis of the global metagenomic data.

claim: Streptomyces sp. WAC04657 is a cosmopolitan phz+ species that commonly appears in both soil and rhizosphere samples.
source: Higher-resolution analysis of the mapped phenazine biosynthesis genes suggests Streptomyces sp. WAC04657 is a cosmopolitan phz+ species that commonly appears in both soil and rhizosphere samples (Figure 3D–E).
evidence: This is a finding from the species-level taxonomic analysis.

claim: Seven Streptomyces species are >2 fold enriched in plant-associated samples.
source: Furthermore, we find seven Streptomyces species that are >2 fold enriched in plant-associated samples.
evidence: This is a finding from the comparative analysis of soil vs. rhizosphere samples.

claim: The genomes of five of the seven rhizosphere-enriched Streptomyces contain the mevalonate pathway for phenazine prenylation.
source: Intriguingly, the genomes of five of these Streptomyces contain the mevalonate pathway for phenazine prenylation (Figure 3E–F), implying these particular types of phenazines could be globally enriched in rhizosphere microbiomes.
evidence: This is a finding from the genomic analysis with an inference about global distribution.

claim: Low levels of other phz+ actinobacteria such as Streptosporangiales and Pseudonocardiales are common in many habitats.
source: In addition to Streptomyces, low levels of other phz+ actinobacteria such as Streptosporangiales and Pseudonocardiales are common in many habitats (Figure 4B; Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the taxonomic analysis of the global metagenomic data.

claim: Pseudomonas is detected at high levels almost exclusively in Washington wheat samples.
source: For example, Pseudomonas is detected at high levels almost exclusively in our Washington wheat samples and Myxococcales are mainly detected in the barley microbiome (Figure 4—figure supplement 2; Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is a finding from the taxonomic analysis showing habitat specificity.

claim: Myxococcales are mainly detected in the barley microbiome.
source: For example, Pseudomonas is detected at high levels almost exclusively in our Washington wheat samples and Myxococcales are mainly detected in the barley microbiome (Figure 4—figure supplement 2; Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is a finding from the taxonomic analysis showing habitat specificity.

claim: Burkholderiales levels are highest in agricultural field soils.
source: While Burkholderiales are commonly detected, their levels are highest in agricultural field soils (Figure 4—figure supplement 2; Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a finding from the taxonomic analysis showing habitat preference.

claim: The phz+ reference database contains only two distantly related groups belonging to the Xanthomonadales: Lysobacter and Dyella.
source: Our phz+ reference database contains only two distantly related groups belonging to the Xanthomonadales: Lysobacter and Dyella (Figure 1C; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a description of the reference database composition.

claim: phz+ Dyella were only recently isolated from the A. thaliana rhizosphere and were not studied with respect to their putative phenazine biosynthesis capabilities.
source: However, these phz+ Dyella were only recently isolated from the A. thaliana rhizosphere and were not studied with respect to their putative phenazine biosynthesis capabilities (Levy et al., 2018).
evidence: This is background information supported by citation.

claim: The L. antibioticus gene products LaPhzS and LaPhzNO1 catalyze the decarboxylative hydroxylation and N-oxidations of PDC to generate the phenazine iodinin.
source: Specifically, the L. antibioticus gene products LaPhzS and LaPhzNO1 were shown to catalyze the decarboxylative hydroxylation and N-oxidations of PDC to generate the phenazine iodinin (Zhao et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The SAM-dependent O-methyltransferase, LaPhzM, converts iodinin into the highly toxic phenazine, myxin.
source: In addition, the SAM-dependent O-methyltransferase, LaPhzM, was later found to convert iodinin into the highly toxic phenazine, myxin (Jiang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: D. japonica and L. antibioticus have similar gene content and a conserved operonic structure in their phenazine biosynthesis clusters.
source: We compared the biosynthesis clusters of both L. antibioticus and D. japonica and found similar gene content between these organisms, as well as a conserved operonic structure.
evidence: This is a finding from the comparative genomic analysis.

claim: An adjacent putative transcription factor was conserved between L. antibioticus and D. japonica.
source: Notably, an adjacent putative transcription factor (TF) was also conserved between these organisms.
evidence: This is a finding from the comparative genomic analysis.

claim: D. japonica produces the phenazines PDC, myxin, and 1-Hydroxy-6-methoxyphenazine-N10-oxide that were previously described in L. antibioticus.
source: We detected several phenazines previously described in L. antibioticus in the WT cultures but not in the phenazine deficient mutants (Figure 5D). These included the precursor PDC, and the potent antimicrobials myxin and a reduced myxin derivative (1-Hydroxy-6-methoxyphenazine-N10-oxide) (Chowdhury et al., 2012; Weigele et al., 1970; Figure 5D; Figure 5—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is experimental data from LC-MS analysis.

claim: Phosphate limitation has been implicated in the induction of phenazine biosynthesis in P. aeruginosa.
source: In P. aeruginosa, phosphate limitation has been implicated in the induction of phenazine biosynthesis (Whooley and McLoughlin, 1982; similar trends have been seen for other antibiotics made by diverse bacteria [Martín, 1977]).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: D. japonica colonization levels are comparable to strong maize colonizers tested in the gnotobiotic model.
source: These colonization levels are comparable to strong maize colonizers tested in this model (Niu et al., 2017) and are similar to those previously reported for plant growth-promoting Pseudomonas fluorescence in a tomato seedling model (Simons et al., 1996).
evidence: This is a comparison to literature values supported by citations.

claim: Phenazine production in the mono-colonization assay has a slight adverse effect on colonization efficiency.
source: These results suggest that the A. thaliana isolated D. japonica is a robust maize colonizer and that phenazine production in this mono-colonization assay has a slight adverse effect on colonization efficiency.
evidence: This is an inference based on the colonization data comparing WT and mutant strains.

claim: Most crops and agricultural soils are colonized by different phz+ bacteria, the most common of which are Streptomyces.
source: While the majority of research on phenazine production has been in pseudomonads (Chincholkar and Thomashow, 2013), our study demonstrates that most crops and agricultural soils are colonized by different phz+ bacteria, the most common of which are Streptomyces.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the global metagenomic analysis.

claim: Particular Streptomyces species are more common in plant rhizospheres compared with bulk soils.
source: Indeed, our data suggest that particular Streptomyces species are more common in plant rhizospheres compared with bulk soils.
evidence: This is a finding from the comparative analysis of soil vs. rhizosphere samples.

claim: The potential roles of prenylated phenazines in bacterial physiology, root colonization and/or pathogen inhibition are completely unknown.
source: The potential roles of prenylated phenazines in bacterial physiology, root colonization and/or pathogen inhibition are completely unknown and represent an exciting research direction.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge.

claim: Prenylated phenazines could be common in the A. thaliana rhizosphere.
